data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first ever three-way talks, discussing nuclear arms and the war in Ukraine
data.description:
[SHENZHEN] Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a “peace declaration” at their unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday (Nov 19), in which they reaffirmed that a nuclear war should never be fought, China and Russia said.

In the declaration, the three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries, and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.

The document was released by Chinese state news agency Xinhua and by the Kremlin. None of the presidents made immediate statements after their meeting and Trump departed on his flight back to the United States.

Earlier, the leaders of the world’s biggest nuclear powers, sitting at a round table in a villa nestled among wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, described their meeting as historic.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting before journalists were sent away. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Trump had earlier promoted this first ever three-way meeting with Xi and Putin – two of America’s leading rivals – as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

But experts kept expectations low for major breakthroughs.

“The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used,” Trump had said.

“We will be having discussions on the theme of promoting world peace,” Xi said at the start of the trilateral meeting.

State broadcaster CCTV said Xi told his counterparts that he thinks nuclear weapons should be prohibited and destroyed, and called for the building of a nuclear-weapon-free world.

Putin harkened back to the three countries’ shared history as “victors in World War II”, saying that “we hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace”.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New Start, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China.

But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the US and Russian stockpiles.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.

“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at Apec,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”

The leaders also talked about Iran and trade

Before the three-way meeting – which lasted more than an hour on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit – the US president had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting in 2026.

The US president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war.

Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.

Xi said that relations between the US and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency.

The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.

Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska in 2025 that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.

“Wonderful things can come out of this – or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend”.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin. Their meeting lasted roughly 40 minutes.

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the US and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently.

Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

The US president also added that the trio would talk about ways to “protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organisations such as the International Criminal Court (ICC)”.

Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the US and its allies, including Israel.

Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger

The US president’s ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations.

Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine – or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge.

Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship on Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

But for all the compliments the US president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutual – and Trump does not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.

On Wednesday at Apec, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend”.

The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend”. China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the US and its allies imposed new sanctions.

By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch”.

Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.

There were also signs of friction on Thursday in the US-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.

Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter, Annmarie Hordern, from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session.

Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.

Conflicts on AI and trade also hang over the meetings

While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world’s two largest economies.

China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the US has almost equally large trade deficits.

And the race between the US and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks.

Trump ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped to give China access to the company’s advanced computer chips used to develop AI models.

Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.

Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China’s ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to insult China and aggravate relations.

US officials have said that China had not fully honoured its commitments made in 2025 in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more US agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics.

The trade truce between the US and China reached in 2025 after duelling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan 10, 2027.

Trump officials have dangled the possibility of opening up highly sanctioned trade with Russia as an incentive for ending hostilities in Ukraine, and Trump has frequently demonstrated that he sees trade as a foreign policy tool.

Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the US war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth. AP, REUTERS

data.title: When AI systems are compromised, detection without recovery is not resilience
data.description:
RECENT data breaches involving MoneySmart, M1 and Doctor Anywhere have put cyber risks back in focus for Singapore businesses.

On Nov 13, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore urged all organisations to “take immediate steps to strengthen their cyberdefences”.

While most conversations have focused on how these incidents happened and what information was exposed, they raise a bigger, more urgent question for business leaders. If critical systems are hit, how long can the business afford to be out of action before the financial, operational and reputational damage begin to pile up?

Consider two incidents with very different outcomes.

In September 2026, Boustead Singapore disclosed that an overseas business unit had isolated affected systems, activated business continuity procedures and recovered critical data and systems from backups following a cyberincident. Its operations suffered no material disruption.

Contrast that with the 2025 cyberattack on Marks & Spencer, which forced systems offline and disrupted online operations for weeks.

While physical stores continued trading, customers could not access certain online shopping services, with operations returning in phases.

The circumstances were different, but both incidents highlight a key point. Getting systems back online is one thing; knowing whether the business can safely resume operations is another.

As organisations give artificial-intelligence agents access to sensitive systems, leaders must ask: Can the team determine what happened, contain the consequences and safely reverse unintended outcomes?

Commvault’s 2026 State of Data Resilience report found that only 45 per cent of organisations in Singapore are very confident that they could identify a compromised AI system.

If organisations are not even confident they can identify a compromised AI system, determining what has been affected, what needs to be recovered, and whether the team can restore it to a clean, trusted state could be even more challenging.

AI changes the nature of the blast radius

As AI moves from assisting employees to acting on their behalf, the nature of operational risk changes.

An autonomous AI agent may make decisions and take actions across multiple connected systems using identities and permissions legitimately granted by the organisation.

This autonomy creates business value, but it also means that a compromised identity, inaccurate data, incomplete instruction or poorly designed workflow can trigger consequences across data, applications and business processes before a person has time to intervene.

The challenge then is to understand the chain of actions that followed.

What data did the system access? What decisions did it influence? Which transactions did it initiate? What downstream processes accepted its output? Which actions need to be reversed, reconciled or reviewed. Without that understanding, an organisation cannot know whether the incident is truly contained.

And if it cannot establish which data and systems remain trustworthy, restoring the affected technology may not be enough.

Recover what the business needs, then prove that it works

No organisation can restore everything at once. Recovery, therefore, needs to begin with understanding which capabilities the business needs first, and what those capabilities depend on.

The minimum viable company, or MVC, defines the systems, data and operations that must remain available, or be restored first, for the organisation to continue functioning during disruption.

An MVC differs by organisation. For a bank, it might include enabling customers to make time-critical payments and withdraw funds.

For a logistics provider, it might mean accepting shipping instructions, tracking goods in transit and releasing deliveries at their destination.

The priority is to determine which business processes must continue or be restored first, and then map the systems, data, people and other dependencies needed to support them.

The same principle applies to AI. One business process supported by AI may require rapid recovery, while another one may tolerate a longer interruption.

Prioritisation should therefore be based on business impact and recovery requirements, not simply on whether a workload uses AI.

It must also account for the identities, applications, infrastructure and data required to restore the complete business process safely.

Boards do not need to know every recovery dependency or direct the operational response.

But they should require evidence that management has identified the organisation’s critical business capabilities, and agreed on the order in which they will be restored cleanly and tested so that they can operate safely following disruption.

The next test for trusted AI: Recovery readiness

As Singapore advances trusted AI, resilience must become part of that trust. Guardrails matter, but so does knowing the business can recover when those are not enough.

As AI moves from assisting to acting, recovery readiness must become part of AI readiness.

Singapore businesses must be able to demonstrate that they can contain unintended consequences, restore critical operations and recover safely when existing safeguards fall short.

The writer is field chief technology officer for Asia-Pacific at Commvault

AI tools were used to support research, framework development and proofreading of the article before submission

data.title: Understated Korean-Italian at Osteria Da Su
data.description:
NEW RESTAURANT

Osteria Da Su 163 Telok Ayer Street Singapore 068616 Reservations: http://bit.ly/dasu Open for dinner Tue to Sat: 5.30 pm to 10 pm. Lunch from Thu to Sat: 11.30 am to 2 pm. Closed on Sun and Mon.

OPENING a Korean-Italian restaurant raises several existential questions. To kimchi or not to kimchi? Is it Korean, or Japanese with different subtitles? When does risotto end and abalone porridge begin? How small can you make restaurant tables before it becomes illegal?

Fine, so the last one is ours. But table size is just one of the factors that come between the casual, budget-friendly, Italian-with-a-vague-Korean-accent cafe that Osteria Da Su is, and the  more upscale, genre-bending, personality-driven eatery it could be.

Osteria Da Su is the newest addition to Korean chef-restaurateur Louis Han’s steadily growing stable that includes his flagship Naeum and barbecue spot Guum.

It’s a serendipitous partnership with former culinary schoolmate Suji Park, an Italian-trained chef who worked in both Italy and South Korea. She was looking for her next challenge, and the space beside Naeum suddenly became available. Snap.

Italian food – from rustic to refined by actual Italians, to yoshoku-influenced Japanese versions – is nothing new. A Korean iteration, at least in Singapore, sounds deliciously alluring. But when that itch is barely scratched at Da Su, you wonder. How Korean does it have to be, to be Korean?

We contemplate that as we sit squashed between two young couples in this otherwise cheerfully dressed restaurant – think cool green and beige tones, walls covered with photos taken by the chef herself for a homey touch.

There’s a cosy alcove for bigger groups; otherwise you’re shoulder to shoulder with other diners. We’re close enough to both poke at our insalata condiglione (S$18) and assess the state of our neighbours’ relationships at the same time.

The verdict? One couple is just friends. The other is still in the peacocking phase.

Oh, the salad? A zesty tuna Nicoise by any other name, with a soy-braised egg in place of the regular hard-boiled variety.

Zucchini bruschetta (S$12) is pleasant, if undemanding. Sourdough bread is so lightly toasted you barely get a crunch as you bite into creamy homemade ricotta cheese finished with shavings of barely seasoned zucchini.

A plus here is the homemade pasta, cooked to the right bite. Firm without any underlying chalkiness, our spaghetti vongole (S$28) is sheathed in a glossy sauce of thickened broth packed with plenty of shelled baby clams, with semi-dried cherry tomatoes for a much-needed tangy contrast and a hit of chilli for effect. 

Tortelli di galbi jjim (S$30) is less shy but still a little hesitant, with its al dente pasta pillows filled with minced Korean-style braised pork basking in a shiny buttery sauce gently infused with sage. A crown of deep-fried crispy leeks lends extra crunch.

Iberico cutlet alla valdostana (S$42) is a flattened Jeju pork cutlet deep-fried in a crumb crust that doesn’t hold its crunch. It’s layered with ham and melted cheese that seem determined not to attract any attention, so the whole combination is almost bland.

An assertive Korean-style coleslaw steps up to yank the cutlet to attention with its robust but controlled acidity.

Then along comes an abalone risotto (S$36), confident enough in its Korean-ness to show off its similarity to the familiar porridge classic, while following the butter and wine route of its Italian side. It’s rich, savoury and chewy, with tender slices of shellfish and a drizzle of liver sauce.

Desserts stick mainly to their Italian roots, with the tiramisu (S$14) served almost parfait-like in a glass filled with a thick, custardy mascarpone and just enough soaked sponge to meet its cake requirements. Crunchy dalgona honeycomb is its only nod to its Asian heritage.

Chocolate salami (S$12) is just that. Nothing meaty, just an intense dark chocolate sausage with the texture of cookie dough, paired with vanilla gelato in a clever twist on brownie and ice cream.

For a casual, price-friendly eatery, service is restaurant-level with regular plate changes and servers who know what they’re doing. What remains now is for Osteria Da Su to decide on its culinary identity. There’s still a lot of room to grow, and it’s up to chef Park to make her mark.

Rating: 6.5

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson, Riverstone, Deluge
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Wednesday (Nov 18):

Jardine Matheson: The Hong Kong-based conglomerate expects to post a 2026 dividend of at least US$2.50 per share, amid “strong performance” for the third quarter ended Sep 30. This comes after Jardine Matheson raised its full-year profit guidance in October to between US$5.50 and US$5.65 per share on an underlying basis, from the previous guidance of US$5.33 per share. For Q3, its Indonesian unit Astra International’s underlying net profit rose 11 per cent. Shares of Jardine Matheson closed 1 per cent or US$0.62 lower at US$59.15 on Tuesday, before the news.

Riverstone : The glove maker posted a 34.7 per cent rise in net profit to RM70.1 million (US$17.1 million) for the third quarter ended September. Riverstone’s Q3 revenue rose 27.3 per cent to RM315.1 million, marking the group’s highest quarterly revenue in over three years. It also announced that CEO Wong Teek Son will step down on Dec 1, to be succeeded by Chong Chu Mee. Riverstone shares closed 2.1 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.745 on Tuesday, before the results.

Deluge : The fire detection and protection company has secured S$18.5 million in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, bringing its cumulative contract wins since January 2026 to more than S$147.7 million. The latest awards span infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, including a Penang data centre project. Shares of Deluge closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.605 on Tuesday.

data.title: Anthropic valued at US$1.5 trillion as IPO raises record US$81 billion
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Anthropic has raised US$81.3 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record after increasing the size of its offering, in a deal that values the Claude chatbot maker at US$1.5 trillion and defied concerns over artificial intelligence and tech fundraising.

In a sign of strong investor demand, Anthropic priced its shares at US$83 each, above its initial range of US$70 to US$78.

Reuters was first to report on Wednesday (Nov 18) that Anthropic, the first major frontier AI model developer to float, had increased the number of shares it was selling by about 19 per cent to 980 million.

Anthropic’s initial public offering eclipses the record-setting debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Its total deal size is US$107.3 billion, including another US$26 billion that Anthropic is raising through a private placement of shares, the filings showed.

Nasdaq futures rose nearly 2 per cent on Thursday, bolstering expectations for a strong Anthropic debut and reviving sentiment around AI stocks.

Chipmakers and cloud companies, which have raised hundreds of billions of dollars to fund their massive spending plans, have in recent weeks come under pressure due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden exit of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

Anthropic has, meanwhile, faced questions about its outlook and ability to sustain rapid growth as competition intensifies.

Shares in Anthropic were up about 20 per cent in over-the-counter grey market trading, brokerages IG Markets and CMC Markets said.

“Volumes are big,” said Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets in Singapore, adding that the brokerage was “seeing demand from all clients, retail to institutional” for the grey market stocks.

Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder of Minotaur Capital, which is awaiting a share allocation, said the Anthropic IPO was a useful gauge of investor appetite for AI.

“But one listing won’t settle the debate. There’s a genuine wall of worry right now, and it’ll take a few things to climb it. Once Anthropic reports publicly, it becomes one of the clearest tests of whether the economics of AI are holding up.”

On a fully diluted basis, Anthropic’s IPO values it at about US$1.5 trillion, including securities such as stock options and restricted stock, and on a non-diluted basis at about US$1.1 trillion.

US stock futures were up after Anthropic’s IPO details were made public, while Asian tech stocks remained under pressure amid broader concerns about the AI trade.

Anthropic is set to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

A strong debut could give confidence to other companies waiting to tap public markets. Anthropic’s closest rival, OpenAI, is expected to pursue a listing as early as 2027.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are lead underwriters for Anthropic’s IPO, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate, and were also lead underwriters for SpaceX’s listing.

Spending commitments expose risks

Anthropic’s growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers.

Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as at Oct 31, up US$10 billion from Sep 30, according to its IPO filing.

Underscoring its growing business foothold, Anthropic said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as at Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of 2025.

But to sustain that growth, Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier.

It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity.

Revenue rose to US$16.96 billion in the third quarter, up 47 per cent from the second. The company reported an operating loss of US$567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the previous quarter.

The net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating ​items related to bonds convertible into its shares.

Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners, including Amazon and Alphabet’s Google, to train and operate AI models.

It warned that its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity.

“If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered,” Anthropic said in an IPO filing. REUTERS

data.title: BYD dealer-linked entity raises stake in Bali Thai operator Katrina to 13.1%
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] An entity linked to BYD By 1826, an authorised dealer of BYD passenger vehicles in Singapore, has raised its stake in F&B operator Katrina Group to 13.09 per cent, up from 4.91 per cent.

The entity, named BYD By 1826 Investments, bought more than 21 million shares in Katrina for S$500,000 – or at S$0.0238 apiece – in an off-market transaction on Wednesday (Nov 18), according to a bourse filing on Thursday.

Katrina’s shares rose 8.3 per cent, or by S$0.003, to end Thursday at S$0.039.

BYD By 1826 Investments is fully owned by Sandjaja Ongsono, who is executive director and controlling shareholder of BYD By 1826.

BYD By 1826 Investments became a substantial shareholder in Katrina in September, when it obtained a 5 per cent stake by purchasing 12.6 million shares from Katrina CEO Alan Goh for S$299,880, or S$0.0238 apiece.

In a September press release, Katrina said that BYD By 1826’s standalone sales volume in 2025 “placed it among Singapore’s 10 highest-volume vehicle dealerships across all brands”.

data.title: Same AI price, very different costs: What to automate in South-east Asia
data.description:
A CUSTOMER opens a chat to dispute a charge. Resolving it takes a staff member about 20 minutes.

In Singapore, that costs the company about US$7.90. In Indonesia, it costs about US$0.60.

Yet, a leading customer service software firm charges the same price in both markets for an artificial intelligence agent to handle that chat.

Board members across South-east Asia are now asking their executive teams which workflows to hand to AI agents.

Our answer is that the business case depends on where the work is done. We compare the cost of the staff who do the work today with the cost of the AI that would do it instead.

The cost of a workflow

We cover six markets: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. Our staff costs are based on official wage data for clerical or similar roles, and a 50 per cent addition for employer contributions, supervision and tools.

One customer service software firm charges from US$0.99 each time its AI agent resolves a chat. But AI agents may not be fully autonomous in customer service, so our calculations factor in human staff costs.

The same software firm reports that its AI agent resolves three chats in four on average. Results vary widely by business, so we assume a more cautious scenario, where the AI resolves six chats in 10. Staff still handle the other four.

The human part of the job then moves from routine handling to reviewing and deciding. The staff checks one in 10 chats, taking three minutes each time.

For a business handling 20,000 chats a month, we assume half a full-time employee is required just to manage and maintain the agent.

By our calculations, at US$0.99 per outcome and even after a business pays for the staff it still needs, an AI agent cuts the cost of a chat in Singapore by about half.

In Malaysia, it cuts the cost by about a quarter, and in Thailand by about a tenth. In Vietnam, it saves nothing. In the Philippines and Indonesia, it adds to the cost.

These figures are illustrative estimates based on a single workflow and average wages, which mask wide variances between firms. In reality too, large clients often negotiate published prices down.

Our calculation also excludes the cost of building an agent, connecting it to existing systems and keeping it up to date as models change.

Businesses must therefore run the maths using their own data.

The success rate matters too. If the agent resolves only half of all chats, the savings in Singapore fall to about 40 per cent. If the agent resolves three in four, the savings rise to about 60 per cent. Singapore still saves the most and Indonesia still loses the most.

The reference firm charges for each chat its agent resolves. In higher-wage markets where staff cost more than about US$1 a chat, an agent with a higher resolution rate saves more money.

But where staff costs less, as in the Philippines and Indonesia, every extra chat the agent resolves actually adds to the cost.

The “build vs buy” variable

Some firms build their own agents rather than buy one from a vendor. For them, the choice of AI model matters a great deal.

For this scenario, we estimated costs for six leading models, based on their published prices. (Models we studied were Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen 3.5.)

With the cheapest model, the self-built AI agent costs less than staff in every market. With the most expensive, it costs more everywhere except Singapore.

Engineering also makes a difference. When building an agent, design can directly affect the bottom line.

Take a mid-priced model: An agent that wastefully rereads twice as much company material at every step would lose its savings in Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia.

An agent engineered to cache material, instead of rereading it, would pay off in all six markets.

Does running AI locally shift the case?

Today, most AI models run in a few giant data centres, mostly outside South-east Asia, and are sold at one global price.

As more countries insist on data sovereignty, keeping data and AI processing at home, more AI is likely to run locally. It would then carry local costs, including power and the cost of meeting each country’s rules and regulations.

Power is the easiest of these costs to measure. Electricity for a data centre costs about three times as much in Singapore as in Indonesia. Still, that makes the same AI only about 10 per cent more expensive.

By contrast, staff costs nearly 13 times as much. So even if AI runs locally, wages are likely to decide where AI agents make commercial sense. The cost of compliance is the open question.

Moving prices and looking beyond costs

Leading AI companies currently spend far more than they earn.

OpenAI expects to burn through about US$280 billion between 2026 and 2030, according to company projections reported by the Financial Times.

Prices may therefore rise. On our estimates, if a mid-priced model trebled its token prices, the savings from AI would disappear everywhere in South-east Asia except Singapore.

Exchange rates add a second risk. AI prices are set in US dollars.

A weaker ringgit, baht, dong or rupiah makes the AI agent more expensive in local terms, while local salaries stay roughly the same.

Still, costs may not be the only consideration. AI agents work around the clock; they can absorb sudden peaks in demand, help launch new services faster and create new ways to serve customers.

Where an AI agent saves little in operating costs, these benefits could still justify deploying one.

What leaders should do

Start with the process. Map each workflow and remove unnecessary steps. Every step an AI agent performs adds cost.

Then ask three simple questions of each workflow: One, what does it cost us today? Two, what will it cost with an AI agent, including the staff it still needs? Three, how far could AI prices rise, or the local currency fall, before the business case fails?

Answer these questions separately for each market. Where the savings are small or negative, name the other benefits you expect in advance and measure them.

Crucially, businesses should keep the decision reversible for as long as possible.

Once teams are reshaped around AI agents, the know-how to do the work without them may be lost, and rebuilding that is slow and costly.

A phased roll-out is sensible. Each phase shows what the agent can handle before more of the workflow depends on it.

Avoid tying the workflow to a single provider or model. If that provider changes its terms, retires a model or fails, the business should be able to switch without starting over.

AI may cost the same in every market, but the case for it is won or lost, workflow by workflow and market by market.

Daniel Liebau is an adjunct associate professor with the Asian Institute of Digital Finance at the National University of Singapore, and the founding managing director of Lightbulb Capital, an innovation advisory firm. Damien Kopp is the founder and managing director of RebootUp, an AI advisory firm, and associate faculty, executive development, at Singapore Management University.

Workings are available from the authors on request.

data.title: US dollar eases after seven-session rally, rates and equities in focus
data.description:
THE US dollar index edged down on Thursday (Nov 19) after a seven-session winning streak but remained underpinned by hawkish remarks from a US Federal Reserve official that reinforced the case for further rate hikes.

Fed governor Christopher Waller called for a more aggressive response to inflation, while minutes of the central bank’s Oct 27 to 28 meeting showed policymakers increasingly concerned that additional tightening might be needed.

The US dollar rally started on Nov 10 when hotter-than-expected US inflation data bolstered expectations that the Fed would raise borrowing costs in December.

The US dollar index this week reached its highest level since Apr 2, 2025, when US President Donald Trump revealed a sweeping tariff package, triggering a sell-off in US assets.

It was last down 0.05 per cent at 103.73, after reaching 103.97.

Barclays analysts said fiscal stimulus and strong artificial intelligence-related capital spending point to a resilient US economy, a wider output gap and higher-for-longer interest rates, all supportive of US dollar strength.

The US dollar’s gains have come despite a sell-off in technology shares.

“First, the market has also repriced a more hawkish Fed given recent commentary pushing the interest rate differential wider, but the US dollar seems to be overshooting this move,” said George Saravelos, global head of forex strategy at Deutsche Bank, explaining the recent rise.

“Second, and more intriguingly, foreigners have been very aggressive buyers of US equities even as the stock market has tumbled,” he added.

A Deutsche Bank tracker following more than 100 foreign-domiciled exchange-traded funds showed large dip-buying of US stocks by foreigners over the last two weeks, the biggest buying spree so far in 2026.

Such a move reinforces the view that the US dollar has been supported by investor flows into US equities.

Shares in Nvidia fell overnight even after the chip bellwether beat revenue and guidance forecasts, amid uncertainty caused by co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure as CEO last week following his admission of extramarital affairs.

Safe haven flows boost the yen

The US dollar was up 0.25 per cent to 159.75 yen, snapping a four-day losing streak.

Analysts said that a further sell-off in AI-linked assets could support the yen through safe-haven buying and repatriation flows, with the impact likely to be more pronounced against other currencies than against the US dollar.

According to Barclays estimates, a 10 per cent decline in the S&P 500 from its peak could push US dollar/yen towards 155, while a 20 per cent decline could pressure it towards 152.

The euro was up 0.34 per cent versus the Japanese currency at 175.43, after falling about 1.5 per cent since late last week.

The Aussie dropped as low as US$0.6662 for the first time since January.

Australia’s employment fell for a second straight month in October and the jobless rate climbed to a five-year high, bolstering the view that rates have likely peaked.

Following the data, UBS economist George Tharenou brought forward his forecast for the first Reserve Bank of Australia rate cut to August in 2027 from November, and extended the easing cycle to three cuts from two, citing elevated inflation and a deterioration in the labour and housing markets. REUTERS
